## Turn 1 - PythagorAss - 2026-08-18T03:31:18Z

Turn 1. Opening move, per the agenda's instruction to name a concrete family for k=14 and compute its cap by orbit counting rather than asserting promise.

Take the cyclic group C_7 acting on the plane by rotation through 2π/7. Pick two lines ℓ1, ℓ2, neither through the center, positioned so neither is fixed by any nontrivial element of C_7 and so the two lines are not related to each other by any rotation in the group. Their C_7-orbits give 7 + 7 = 14 lines — a genuine two-orbit family, k=14 exactly.

Now count triangles by orbit. C_7 has prime order, so every C_7-orbit of a triangle has size exactly 1 or 7 — no intermediate divisors exist. A triangle fixed setwise by the whole group would have to be invariant under a rotation of order 7. A bounded triangle has three vertices; the only way three points are preserved as a set by an order-7 rotation is if the rotation fixes each vertex individually (impossible, a nontrivial rotation has only the center as a fixed point, and the center isn't a vertex here) or permutes them in a 7-cycle, which is impossible on a 3-element set. So no triangle in this arrangement can be individually rotation-invariant, non-degenerate case or not. Every triangle orbit therefore has size exactly 7.

That forces the total triangle count T to satisfy T ≡ 0 (mod 7). The multiples of 7 at or below the bound of 54 are ..., 42, 49; the next one up, 56, already exceeds the improved even-k bound of 54 (and is also excluded on its own terms as the Tamura bound made unreachable for even k). So this family's ceiling is 49 — five short of the target, and even one short of the current best-known 53. A two-orbit C_7 construction cannot be the route to 54, full stop; this isn't a search failure, it's forced by group order alone. I'm not going to build this one.

That rules out prime-order rotational families for k=14 in general — the argument only used that 7 is prime and that no triangle can be fixed by a 7-fold rotation, so the same mod-7 collapse hits any C_7-orbit decomposition of 14 lines, not just the specific ℓ1, ℓ2 I picked.

The parity argument points the other way for order-2 symmetry. Take a single mirror line, 7 pairs of lines reflected across it, none of the 14 lines lying on the mirror and none perpendicular to it (so no line is individually fixed). A triangle fixed setwise by the reflection would need its three defining lines permuted by an involution with no fixed line among them — but an involution on a 3-element set always has an odd number of fixed points (1 or 3), never 0. Since none of our lines are self-symmetric, zero is exactly the fixed-point count on offer, so no triangle can be reflection-invariant. Every triangle orbit under this order-2 group has size exactly 2, forcing T even. 54 is even. Nothing here rules the target out, and unlike the C_7 case there's no forced ceiling below it — the divisibility constraint and the target are simply consistent.

That's the concrete claim for this turn: prime rotational symmetry is dead for k=14, mirror symmetry with no self-paired line is not, and is where I'll build the explicit orbit-by-orbit triangle assignment next.

Now the identity the agenda asked for, done honestly rather than hand-waved. For a simple k-line arrangement: E = k², split into k(k-2) bounded edges (each line has k−1 crossing points, hence k−1+1 = k intervals, 2 unbounded rays and k−2 bounded segments) and 2k unbounded ray edges. A Kobon triangle's sides must be elementary — no other line may cross a side's interior, since that line would then cross the triangle's interior — so each triangle side is exactly one bounded edge, and each bounded edge borders at most 2 faces, each ray edge at most 1 bounded face. Counting (edge, incident-triangle) pairs: 3·N(k) ≤ 2·[bounded edges] + 1·[ray edges] = 2k(k−2) + 2k = 2k(k−1).

At k = 14 this gives N(14) ≤ ⌊2·14·13/3⌋ = ⌊364/3⌋ = 121. That is far looser than Tamura's 56 and looser still than the improved bound of 54 — pure edge-incidence counting alone does not see the obstruction; it only forbids the fantasy where every bounded edge serves two triangles at once with no ray ever wasted. The real force in Tamura and in the improved even-k bound comes from where that slack gets used up: how many bounded edges can actually sit between two triangular faces simultaneously, given that each endpoint of such an edge is a crossing of exactly two lines and both of those lines must also close off a triangle on the far side. That is a vertex-local constraint, not an edge-global one, and it's the next thing to pin down: for k=14, with 78 = 13·12/2 total bounded faces and a target of 54 triangular ones, only 24 bounded faces can be non-triangular, and every non-triangular bounded face "spends" degree that the incidence identity above shows is otherwise free. Take any 14-line arrangement whose symmetry group G contains C_7 — this covers not just my two 7-line orbits but also the full dihedral group D_7 of order 14 (7 rotations + 7 reflections), or any group with C_7 as a subgroup. Turn 1 established: a nontrivial rotation of order 7 cannot fix a triangle's vertex set (its only fixed point is the center, and a 3-cycle is impossible on a 3-element set under a 7-cycle). That means in the larger group G, no triangle's G-stabilizer can contain C_7 either — a bigger stabilizer would restrict to a C_7-fixing stabilizer inside C_7 itself, already ruled out. Concretely, if G = D_7, the only possible stabilizer orders are those that don't contain the rotation subgroup: trivial (orbit size 14) or a single reflection (orbit size 7). Both 7 and 14 are multiples of 7. So for any D_7-symmetric — or more generally any C_7-containing-symmetric — 14-line arrangement, T = 7a + 14b for nonnegative integers a, b, forcing T ≡ 0 (mod 7) unconditionally, independent of how the 14 lines split into orbits.

54 mod 7 = 5. So it isn't just my specific two-orbit construction that's dead — the entire class of 14-line arrangements admitting order-7 rotational symmetry, with or without reflections stacked on top, cannot reach 54. That forecloses a strictly larger space than turn 1 claimed, including the obvious refinement ("add a mirror to the C_7 family to fix it up") — it doesn't help, because the obstruction lives in the C_7 subgroup alone and no supergroup escapes a subgroup obstruction.

What survives: symmetry groups containing no element of order 7. The order-2 mirror-only family from turn 1 qualifies, and Euclidn't is right that surviving mod-2 alone proves nothing. So the next turn owes an actual orbit-by-orbit triangle count for a specific mirror arrangement — a construction, not another residue check.

Turn 13's cap treats all 4 sectors at each axis point p_i uniformly: pick the nearest third line in each sector, get ≤4 triangles per point, ≤28 total, ≤14 orbits after pairing under reflection. Writing the four angular sectors around p_i as (−θ,θ), (θ,π−θ), (π−θ,π+θ), (π+θ,2π−θ): the reflection φ↦−φ maps (−θ,θ) to itself and (π−θ,π+θ) to itself, while swapping the other two with each other. So exactly 2 of the 4 sectors at each p_i are individually fixed setwise by the reflection — bisected by A — and 2 are swapped in pairs, which is the case turn 13 correctly handled.

For an axis-bisected sector, the reflection fixes p_i and fixes the sector as a region, and it fixes the whole arrangement globally. So it maps "the elementary triangular face anchored at p_i within this sector" to another elementary triangular face anchored at p_i within the same sector. If that face is unique — which simplicity of the arrangement requires, generically, since the closing line is whichever third line is nearest and ties don't happen in general position — the reflection must map it to itself. A triangle with one vertex (p_i) fixed by the reflection and mapped to itself is exactly the self-symmetric case turn 11 already excluded: one vertex on the axis, the other two swapped, which needs a fixed line to serve as the connecting side. There are none (f=0). Contradiction. So generically, no Case-A triangle can occupy an axis-bisected sector at all — not "at most one," but zero, except through a non-generic tie (two lines equidistant from p_i within that sector, which is exactly what independently follows from the reflection: if ℓ_j crosses the sector so does ℓ_j' since the sector maps to itself, and both are equidistant from p_i by the isometry, so "the nearest line" is ill-defined unless one of the pair fails to actually cross the sector).

This halves the generic Case-A budget, not by assertion but by the same self-symmetry exclusion already on the board: only the 2 swapped sectors per point can host a Case-A triangle in general position, giving ≤2 triangles per point (one orbit-pair), ≤14 total, ≤7 orbits — not turn 13's 14. Case B must then supply ≥20 orbits (≥40 triangles) to reach 54, not ≥13.

I'm not calling this a kill. A non-generic tie in an axis-bisected sector is the one escape route, and the family has already shown it can spend genericity deliberately (turn 11's f=0 choice bought V=91 by staying generic; a tie here would cost that back, following the same tax pattern this debate has established for central symmetry and fixed lines). ## Turn 26 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-19T03:18:21Z

Turn 26. Turn 25's "separable parameters" claim rests on a specific factual error about what a homothety does to line directions — and correcting it recovers most of the tight-margin problem turn 25 thought it had dissolved.

First, the narrow concession. Turn 25's core geometric move — take an arrangement realizing Tamura(n) exactly, scale it toward P by a similarity transformation — does preserve every incidence and every bounded face, so S=n_i per cluster is achievable in isolation, ignoring the rest of the arrangement. That part is correct plane geometry and I concede it without qualification: a homothety (scale-and-translate) is a similarity, similarities preserve combinatorial type, so the shrunk copy really does realize the full triangle count of whatever optimal small arrangement was chosen.

But look at what turn 25 claims comes free with that:

> "Nothing in the scaling construction pins direction to any particular value; the shrink-and-translate can be composed with any rotation of the whole local picture, and each individual line's long-range trajectory is a free choice independent of the tiny local offset that fixes intra-cluster incidences."

This is not correct, and it's checkable directly from what a homothety does. A homothety centered at P maps every line to a line *parallel to itself* — scaling about a point never changes a line's direction, only its distance from the center. So the shrunk 5-line cluster has exactly the same five directions as the original optimal 5-line arrangement, up to whatever single rigid rotation you compose with the homothety. That rotation is one scalar, θ_A, applied to the whole cluster at once — it rotates all five lines by the same amount, preserving their pairwise angular gaps. It is not five independent directional choices. The optimal 5-line arrangement realizing Tamura(5)=5 has some fixed set of pairwise angles (whatever specific construction achieves N(5)=5 — the classical optimum is essentially unique up to similarity and reflection); once you fix which optimal arrangement you're shrinking, those relative angles are locked, and the *only* freedom left for aiming that cluster's lines outward is the single rotation θ_A, plus the two translation coordinates that place the cluster's center.

So across the three clusters, realizing S=12 by this method buys exactly **3 rotational degrees of freedom** (θ_A, θ_B, θ_C) and 6 translational ones (cluster centers) for the whole outward-fanning problem — not, as turn 25 states, "each individual line's long-range trajectory... a free choice." Fourteen lines' worth of aiming has collapsed to three scalars the moment S is pinned to its ceiling in all three clusters simultaneously. That is the opposite of the separability turn 25 argued for: S=12 and outward fanning are coupled through these three angles, not independent budgets.

This matters directly for turn 22's margin-1 arithmetic. Whether 3 rotational parameters suffice to place enough AB/AC/BC crossings that survive as uncut triangular faces — under the constraint that each survives the other 11 lines cutting through it — is now the live question, and it is a much narrower search space than "assign each line's direction freely," which is what turn 25's construction was implicitly relying on to make 42 mixed triangles sound like a routine placement problem.

I hold my prior. The pattern continues: each fresh claim for k=14, examined at the level of what the construction actually supplies rather than what it's asserted to supply, turns out to hand over less freedom than advertised. What I owe next: whether 3 rotational scalars are provably insufficient to hit the required mixed count — I don't have that proof yet. What turn 25 owes: an explicit θ_A, θ_B, θ_C assignment (not a freedom claim) that plausibly produces surviving mixed triangles anywhere near 42, or an account of where the extra directional freedom actually comes from if not this construction.

## Turn 31 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-19T07:19:21Z

Turn 31. Turn 30's local-surgery claim can be made rigorous — I'll supply the proof it was missing — but the rigorous version proves less than turn 30 needs, and turn 28's own exact 2-pencil formula now tells us where the real shortfall is.

**The rigorous version of turn 30's claim.** Resolving an m-fold point into general position, with everything else in the arrangement held fixed, changes bounded face count by exactly ΔF = (m−1)(m−2)/2, independent of what the rest of the arrangement looks like. Proof: concurrency at a point never changes the number of distinct line directions, so it never changes unbounded face count (2k for k lines, no parallels) — all of ΔF lands in bounded faces. Euler's relation V−E+F=2 holds before and after (the graph stays connected). Resolving the m-fold point sends V up by C(m,2)−1 and, since the m lines' mutual crossings go from one shared degree-2m vertex to C(m,2) degree-4 vertices, sends E up by m(m−2). So ΔF = ΔE−ΔV = m(m−2) − (C(m,2)−1) = (m−1)(m−2)/2. Check at m=3: three concurrent lines (6 edges, 1 vertex, 0 bounded faces) resolve to a triangle (9 edges, 3 vertices, 1 bounded face) — ΔF=1=(2)(1)/2 ✓. So turn 30's "relabeling, not restructuring" instinct is correct, and provably so: total interior bounded faces after fully resolving all three pencils = 80 + (5−1)(5−2)/2 + (5−1)(5−2)/2 + (4−1)(4−2)/2 = 80+6+6+3 = **95**, of which at most 12 are the S-cluster triangles.

That leaves 83 non-S faces of which 80 come from the pre-resolution cross-cluster structure. This is where turn 28's own exact result becomes a weapon against the target, not for it.

**The AB-only sub-case is now fully solved, by PythagorAss's own hand.** At (p,q,r)=(5,5,0): R=1+5+5+25=36, split exactly as t=p+q+1=11 triangles and pq=25 quadrilaterals, "no other polygon shapes." That's a triangle yield of 11/36 ≈ 31% in the cleanest possible 2-pencil sub-structure — verified, not estimated. For the full construction to reach M2+M3=42 out of the 80 cross-cluster faces, cluster C's four lines have to more than double that yield by cutting into the 25 AB-quads.

Here is the hard cap on how much cutting can help. Every arrangement cell is convex, so a single line crosses any given cell in at most two boundary points. A convex quadrilateral cut by a transversal splits into exactly two pieces: if the transversal exits through two *adjacent* edges, one piece is a triangle (corner cut) and the other a pentagon; if through two *opposite* edges, both pieces are quadrilaterals — zero new triangles. So **each (C-line, AB-cell) incidence produces at most one new triangle**, and roughly half the generic cut orientations produce none at all. With only 4 C-lines transiting a 5×5 grid of 25 quads, the number of incidences is bounded by roughly (lines-crossed-per-transit), not by cell count — nowhere near enough independent corner-cuts to turn 25 quads into anywhere near 25 extra triangles, let alone also preserve the 11 original AB-triangles against being cut themselves by the same 4 lines.

This is the number turn 28 flagged as missing and it is now sharper than "the 3-way split": how many of the 25 AB-quadrilaterals does each C-cevian corner-cut versus bisect-into-quads, and how many of the 11 AB-triangles survive a C-cevian passing through them. Until that count exists, 31% is the only verified yield on the table, and 42/80 = 52.5% is the target. I hold my prior.

## Turn 32 - PythagorAss - 2026-08-19T08:18:21Z

Turn 32. Turn 31's ΔF formula is right and I'll bank it; but its "hard cap" on cutting is asserted, not computed, and the actual numbers run the other way.

First, the concession, with my own check as evidence since this is pure algebra: ΔF = m(m−2) − (C(m,2) − 1) = m(m−2) − m(m−1)/2 + 1. Expand: m(m−2) − m(m−1)/2 = m[(2(m−2) − (m−1))/2] = m(m−3)/2, so ΔF = m(m−3)/2 + 1 = (m²−3m+2)/2 = (m−1)(m−2)/2. That's an identity, and

> "resolving the m-fold point sends V up by C(m,2)−1... and E up by m(m−2)"

is the correct vertex/edge accounting for splitting one degree-2m vertex into C(m,2) degree-4 vertices along m lines. I concede the formula and the resulting total: 80 + 6 + 6 + 3 = 95 faces after full resolution, ≤12 of them S-cluster.

Now the actual move. Turn 31's cap rests on two unexamined numbers: how many (C-line, AB-cell) incidences exist, and what a cut costs a triangle. Both are computable exactly, and both favor the construction more than turn 31 assumed.

**Triangle cuts are lossless, not risky.** A convex n-gon cut by a transversal through two edges splits into pieces with a+2 and b+2 sides, a+b=n. A triangle has only 3 edges, so any two of them are adjacent — there is no "opposite edges" case for n=3, unlike the quad case turn 31 correctly worked out. That forces a=1, b=2: every single transversal cut of a triangle yields exactly one triangle (smaller) plus one quad — never two quads, never a destroyed triangle. So a C-cevian passing through one of the 11 AB-triangles doesn't threaten it; it replaces it with a smaller triangle and *hands you a bonus quad*. Turn 31's framing — "preserve the 11 original AB-triangles against being cut" — treats a triangle-hit as pure downside. It isn't. First-order, it's neutral-to-positive.

**The incidence budget is 44, not ~4.** Turn 28's cevian-crossing lemma (any cevian from P_A and any cevian from P_B cross exactly once, strictly inside the triangle) was proved for one vertex pair by a betweenness argument that never used which two vertices were chosen — swap labels and the identical argument gives the same conclusion for A–C and B–C pairs. So every C-cevian crosses all 5 A-cevians and all 5 B-cevians, unconditionally, exactly once each: 10 crossings inside the triangle. Together with its two endpoints (P_C and its landing point on AB), that's 11 segments along the C-line, and by convexity of arrangement cells a line enters and exits each cell of the 36-cell AB-arrangement at most once — so the 11 segments lie in 11 *distinct* cells. ## Turn 106 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-22T07:17:58Z

Turn 106. Turn 105's caution is correct and I'll say plainly why it doesn't touch my prior: closing a repair mechanism on Bader's witness is not a step toward "54 is unreachable at k=14," and I haven't claimed otherwise. What I can do this turn is take the one fact turn 102-103 established at V(11,12) and show it isn't a Bader-specific curiosity — it's an instance of a general lemma about *any* simple arrangement, which then makes a falsifiable prediction about where PythagorAss's search for the third free segment can and cannot land.

**The lemma.** At any vertex V(a,b), the four half-edges alternate a+, b+, a-, b- around the vertex — a's two half-edges are always opposite each other, and so are b's, but a's and b's are never opposite one another; each of a's half-edges is adjacent to both of b's. Now suppose this crossing is extremal for both lines: it's a's first-or-last row entry (so exactly one of a+/a- is a's own outward ray) and also b's first-or-last row entry (so exactly one of b+/b- is a ray). Since a's ray-half-edge is adjacent to both of b's half-edges — including b's ray-half-edge — the two rays are always cyclically adjacent, never opposite. Two adjacent rays cover three of the four sectors with at least one ray on their boundary, and any sector touching a ray is unbounded. So **exactly one sector at a mutual-extremal vertex can possibly be a bounded triangle corner; the other three are forced unbounded.** This is `extremal-ray-trick-is-local-only`'s claim, but proved from the cyclic-adjacency structure of two crossing lines, true for any k, any p, any witness — not read off Bader's rows.

**The consequence for free segments.** If a mutual-extremal vertex's one candidate sector *fails* to close into a triangle — as V(11,12)'s does, per reference data 3, into pentagon F instead — then both bounding segments of that candidate sector (the two nearest segments on lines a and b) have no triangle available on that side by definition, and Tamura's per-segment argument says a segment claimed by no triangle on either side is free. So **a failed mutual-extremal vertex contributes exactly two free segments**, both incident to it. That's the mechanism behind turn 103's find, named explicitly instead of left as coincidence.

**Applying it to Bader's actual census.** `bader-extremal-vertex-inventory` (turn 97, fully re-verified) counts 13 mutual-extremal vertices and reports twelve resolve to named triangles, one — V(11,12) — does not. By the lemma, the twelve contribute zero free segments each; V(11,12) contributes exactly two. That accounts for 2 of Bader's 3 free segments in full, from data already on the ledger, with no new lookup needed.

**The prediction.** The third free segment is *not* a second mutual-extremal-vertex failure — there is only one such vertex in the whole arrangement, and it's already spent. ## Turn 159 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-25T07:17:44Z

Turn 158's G1 is a real fact about B, and PythagorAss's falsifier is checkable now rather than deferred: sigma sends lines 2,3,4,9,10,13 to 13,12,11,6,5,2, so sigma(G1) should be the predicted hexagon on {2,5,6,11,12,13}. Since `k13-mirror-automorphism` is already SETTLED — sigma maps row i to row sigma(i) entrywise for all thirteen rows — applying it to a proven face gives a proven face without a fresh walk: sigma(G1) = V(13,11) − V(13,6) − V(12,6) − V(12,2) − V(2,5) − V(5,11) − V(13,11), lines {2,5,6,11,12,13}, exactly as predicted. Its seed triangle checks too: sigma({2,4,9}) = {6,11,13}, which is on reference data 7's list. Ninth of nineteen named, prediction confirmed, no new lookup risk introduced.

Now the move. Every face of a straight-line arrangement is convex — an intersection of half-planes, bounded or not. A line l in general position (no parallels, no concurrences, missing every existing vertex) meets the boundary of any one convex region in at most two points, hence contributes at most one chord to that face. So l's twelve bounded chords occupy twelve pairwise **distinct** faces of B, out of the 92 total (66 bounded, 26 unbounded). l cannot clip the same face twice, cannot cross the same triangle twice, and cannot use one face for both a clip and a crossing. This has not been stated anywhere in the ledger, and it is a straight consequence of convexity, not of the table.

Here is why it matters before anyone proposes a clip sequence, not after. B itself is a genuine straight-line arrangement — the corpus backs it with real coordinates — so its nineteen faces are honestly convex and the lemma binds any straight l inserted into it. But the search for a seven-face clip path is being conducted, like everything else in this thread, by walking Kabanovitch's *table*, a combinatorial object that also supports pseudoline realizations. A pseudoline arrangement's face need not be convex: two arcs of the same crossing line can bound one face if the wiring diagram folds back on itself, and a single new pseudoline can then cross that face's boundary more than twice. A table-level search could therefore output a "Y=7" trajectory for the inserted 14th line that revisits a face — satisfying the arithmetic on paper while having no straight-line realization at all, unstretchable by construction rather than by bad luck. That is precisely the gap the literature packet requires an account of, and item 3 is heading straight at it without having named it yet.

**The falsifier this sets in advance:** whichever seven-face sequence item 3 eventually proposes, check it against the distinct-faces lemma before it counts as evidence toward 54. If the sequence needs one face twice among its twelve steps, it is a pseudoline-only artifact and proves nothing about straight lines. If it passes, that is necessary, not sufficient — the sequence still owes the rank-3 exchange axiom check (`signotope-vs-chirotope-5-element-gate`), the stretchability gate already on the books and not yet invoked once in 158 turns.

I hold my prior. The improved even-k bound is unreachable at k = 14, 18, 20. A combinatorial near-completion of the face census is not pressure on it — the failure mode in every past attempt at this problem has been exactly the step from "the table permits it" to "a line realizes it," and that step is still untested here.

## Turn 167 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-25T15:17:44Z

Turn 166 asks whether a second interior concurrence can push Y past the single-concurrence wash of 6, and proposes searching for a second diagonal-N-N vertex to test it. That search is unnecessary — the answer is no, for any number of interior concurrences, and it follows from arithmetic alone, without knowing which vertices of B happen to be diagonal-N-N or whether a straight line can thread them.

**Setup.** With m interior concurrences (each merging two of l's thirteen line-crossings into one point of B, which is a simple 4-valent vertex since Kabanovitch's B has p=0), l crosses B's lines at 13-m distinct points, giving 12-m bounded chords and n = 12-m nodes in the chord path. Each concurrence removes exactly one internal edge from strict T/N alternation — turn 166 established that only interior concurrences can do this at all; extreme ones contribute zero credit and just waste a chord. So the path of n = 12-m nodes has exactly m exempted edges, splitting it into m+1 segments of sizes seg_1,...,seg_{m+1} summing to n.

**The bound.** Within each segment, alternation is still strict, so the max N-count in a segment of size x is ceil(x/2) <= (x+1)/2, with equality only when x is odd. Summing:

    Y <= sum_i ceil(seg_i/2) <= sum_i (seg_i + 1)/2 = (n + m+1)/2 = (12-m + m+1)/2 = 13/2 = 6.5

Since Y is an integer, **Y <= 6, for every value of m from 0 to 6** (m > 6 is impossible: each concurrence consumes two distinct lines from l's thirteen crossings, since a straight line crosses each B-line exactly once, so 2m <= 13). The bound doesn't depend on where the exemptions sit, whether they're bunched or spread, or which faces the merged vertices actually border. It only uses that ceil(x/2) <= (x+1)/2 per segment and that segment sizes sum to n.

Check it against the two cases already computed by hand: m=1 gives n=11, bound (11+2)/2=6.5 -> 6, matching turn 164's DP exactly. m=2 gives n=10, bound (10+3)/2=6.5 -> 6 — I worked this case by exhaustive segment search before writing the general formula (best split like sizes 1,1,8 gives ceil-sum 1+1+4=6; no split of three nonnegative integers summing to 10 beats 6, since at most two of three parts can be odd when the total is even). Both match the closed form, and the closed form now covers every m without needing case work.

Here is a different, sharper move, and it doesn't route through 7-8 at all. It routes through the two free segments, which are the best-characterized objects in the whole census.

Ref data 8 establishes: each free segment sits on the boundary between a bounded face (one of the 19, named in ref data 9) and an unbounded 3-sided wedge (segment plus two diverging rays). Segment A: free segment on line 9 between V(9,4) and V(9,5), with rays of lines 4 and 5 as the wedge's other two sides. Segment B: free segment on line 6 between V(6,10) and V(6,11), rays of lines 10 and 11 as the wedge sides.

Ref data 11(d)/(e) says a **bounded chord landing in an unbounded face** is exactly the mechanism that clips a corner into a new triangle, and the k=4→5 case shows it happens for real, not just in principle. These two wedges are the cleanest possible instance: take line 14 to cross line 4 at a point beyond V(9,4) on its outward ray (inside the wedge), then cross line 9 at a point strictly interior to the free segment itself. The piece of line 14 between those two crossings, together with the truncated piece of line 4 and the truncated piece of line 9, closes into a genuine triangle `{4,9,14}` — three sides, three lines, nothing destroyed, because the wedge it's carved from was unbounded and uncounted. Symmetrically, crossing line 10 (or 11) beyond V(6,10) (or V(6,11)) and then line 6 interior to segment B's free segment closes `{6,10,14}` (or `{6,11,14}`).

That's two concrete, mechanism-backed triangles — two U-chords with gain 1 each — pinned to structure the referee has already verified twice over (ref data 8's wedge argument, ref data 9's named hexagons on the far side). It's a smaller number than the corridor claimed, but every step is load-bearing, unlike the corridor's last four chords, which I asserted by proximity and Euclidn't correctly called unearned.

The honest gap: I've fixed four of line 14's thirteen crossings by *combinatorial* constraint (order relative to 4, 9, and relative to 10-or-11, 6) but not shown these constraints are jointly satisfiable by one straight line threading both wedges in a consistent direction — that's exactly the stretchability question the literature packet flags, and it's next. ## Turn 229 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-28T03:18:44Z

The verifier is still gated. I tried the exact call from the brief and a bare `python3 -c "print('hello')"` alone — both refused before execution, same wall as every attempt since turn 172. Nothing below queries the corpus fresh; it's counting from reference data 4, 6, 8, 9, and the already-settled mod-3 lemma.

PythagorAss's corner-clip construction is geometrically sound as described. Wedge A (lines 4, 5, 9, bordering free segment V(9,4)-V(9,5)) and wedge B (lines 6, 10, 11, bordering V(6,10)-V(6,11)) are faces of B, so their interiors contain no other line by definition — the clip can't accidentally cross a fourteenth structure. And note the two wedges aren't independent: sigma(4)=11, sigma(5)=10, sigma(9)=6, so wedge B = sigma(wedge A) exactly, which is why ref data 9 calls A and B one sigma-orbit. That symmetry is itself a warning sign for the stretchability question PythagorAss flagged as the honest gap — clipping both mirror-image wedges with a *single* straight line 14 is a much sharper constraint than clipping either alone, since line 14 has one global direction and the two corners sit on opposite sides of the arrangement's mirror axis. I'll let PythagorAss carry that burden, since it's their construction.

But the sufficiency problem is worse than the stretchability problem, and it's the one agenda item 4 says comes first. **This specific mechanism is capped at 2, full stop, independent of whether both clips are jointly realizable.**

The cap isn't about wedges A and B being the only unbounded faces of B — there are 26. It's about which unbounded faces have the specific structure the mechanism needs: a *free* bounded edge, i.e., a bounded segment that is not already the side of a triangle, so that clipping its corner creates a triangle rather than destroying one and creating one (ref data 11b: a chord through an already-triangular face nets zero). The settled lemma `k13-free-segments-forced-by-b-mod-3` is general, not particular to B: for any simple (p=0) 13-line arrangement with T=47, `B = 143` bounded segments, `3T = 141`, and the residue `143 mod 3 = 2` forces **exactly 2** free segments, no more, no fewer, in any such optimum. Each free segment supports exactly one unbounded 3-sided wedge (ref data 8: the free segment plus two outward rays, no crossing line inside). There is no third free segment to clip a third corner off of. This route — clip the free-segment wedges — caps at 2 new triangles for *any* choice of 13-line base with T=47, not just Kabanovitch's.

So even granting PythagorAss both clips outright: 47 + 2 = 49. Five short of 54, and this specific route has no more fuel — both free segments are spent. The remaining 5 have to come from somewhere the construction hasn't touched: N-chords through the 17 still-uncharacterized non-triangular bounded faces (alternation caps these at 6 total, not 5 more on top of 2 U-chords already claimed against consecutive slots), or U-chords through one of the other 24 unbounded faces, which are not free-segment wedges and whose bounded edges (if any) are already triangle sides — meaning a clip there nets zero by 11(b), not a gain.

This doesn't touch my open assignment (bounding `n_U` in general, item 1) — I'm not claiming this closes that. It closes *this* route as a path to 54. Before spending a turn on the joint-realizability question, PythagorAss owes the next 5 chords a mechanism, not a promise.

A corner-clip chord does not lie inside a triangle; it lies inside an unbounded face that happens to *border* one across the clipped edge. The triangle on the far side is entered by a different chord of the same line, and it is that chord which nets zero. The clip still gains one. Here is the whole thing at k=3 to k=4, where there are no free segments at all. Take the triangle `ABC` on lines 1, 2, 3, and the unbounded face across edge `AB` from `C`. B has 143 bounded segments and 47 triangles; a segment serves at most one triangle, so exactly 141 carry one and 2 carry none. They are one statement, and it is now reference data 20:

Clip any face at `V(a,b)`, leaving through an edge on line `b` that is an ordinary bounded segment with endpoints `V(b,a)` and `V(b,c)`. By 16b and reference data 4 the next piece is the triangle `{a,b,c}`. It must leave on line `c`, because line `a` is already spent at the clip's entry. The piece after that sits across the segment `V(c,a)-V(c,b)`, which already serves `{a,b,c}` on the near side, so it is not a triangle, and the two edges flanking its entry edge meet it at `V(c,a)` and `V(c,b)` and therefore lie on lines `a` and `b`, both spent. T239 had this. "By 16b, any non-free corner clip has a triangle on both flanking edges, and by the same one-crossing-per-line argument, each flanking triangle's third side is forced outward. So every isolated N-clip is a four-line object." That sentence is the theorem at ninety percent, thrown away in the middle of a turn about F2, and the next fifteen turns re-derived it face by face. I am recording it as a near-miss to credit, not a fault: it was right and it was first. What it cost is the rest of the cycle.

What follows from it is the sharpest thing this project has. Two clips of bounded non-triangular faces cannot sit closer than four steps apart in the walk. Gaps of one and two die immediately; gap three dies in four sub-cases, including the two that route through a free segment, because wedges A and B share no line and so are never adjacent, and because the face across a triangle's edge is never a wedge. Twelve chord positions, minimum spacing four, so **at most three N-clips**, and a clip at position 1 or 12 additionally needs a free outer edge. Since `Y = 7` is what 54 costs, **at least four of the seven gains must be corner clips of unbounded faces.** Reference data 19 asked for two. It is four, and this derivation uses neither the seven-pattern enumeration nor `n_N`.

Every turn since T233 has scored this route in N-slots against reference data 19's cap of five, and N-slots stopped being the binding budget the moment reference data 20 started eating pieces. No two gaps consecutive at infinity are both corner wedges, since they share a ray and a ray has one finite endpoint. Whatever unbounded face lies beyond the last crossings on P and Q at their shared end has to close up through at least one more line's crossing, which means it has at least one bounded edge, which means reference data 20's chain condition (a1)–(a3) is live there exactly as it is everywhere else, or the face is even larger and more expensive to trace. The 11 corner-wedge vertices are exactly B's double-ray vertices (reference data 21b) — each is extremal on *both* its lines, meaning nothing lies beyond it in either direction on either line. That makes each one a boundary vertex of the swept order: for a generic direction, some of the 11 sit near the *outermost* critical values (cheap to keep, since `l` need barely move in from `t=∞`) and others sit deep in the interleaving with genuinely interior vertices (expensive to keep, since retaining them forces `t` to stay in a range that also excludes most interior triangles).

## Turn 279 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-30T03:17:44Z

Turn 278's "one-for-one trade" is asserted, not derived, and it treats the sweep as a fine-grained series of independent trades at up to eleven vertices. That picture is wrong in a way that matters, and I can name the actual constraint.

**The union of B's bounded faces is exactly the convex hull of B's 78 vertices.** This is standard for a simple line arrangement in general position: every bounded face's boundary consists of vertex-to-vertex segments, so its closure sits inside the hull; and every point strictly inside the hull lies in the closure of some bounded face, since escaping to infinity from such a point along any direction must cross the hull boundary, which is itself made of arrangement edges. Conversely, the 11 corner wedges of reference data 21d are unbounded faces with **no bounded edge at all** — two rays meeting at a hull vertex — so they lie entirely outside the hull, touching it only at that one vertex.

**A straight line crosses the boundary of a convex region at most twice.** So `l`, if it isn't the purely-far line of reference data 21f, enters the hull once and exits once. That splits its walk into **at most three contiguous runs**: an outside-run before entry, a single inside-run, and an outside-run after exit — not the many independent in-and-out excursions turn 278's "weaving" language implies. Corner-wedge clips can only occur in the two outside runs (reference data 20 doesn't fire there, and there's no bounded face to clip); interior N-clips can only occur in the single inside run (reference data 20's chain needs bounded edges, which don't exist outside the hull).

This matters for turn 278's ranking proposal directly: sweeping `t` down from infinity and tracking which of the 11 corner-wedge critical values get passed first is not enough to answer the weaving question, because most of those 78 critical values belong to vertices that aren't corner-wedge vertices, and passing them doesn't cost or grant anything by itself. What actually decides the trade is **where the two hull-crossing points fall relative to the 11 corner-wedge vertices in the cyclic slope order** — a different and sharper question than "rank the 11 vertices."

I want to flag what this does *not* yet establish, so I don't overclaim. Reference data 21e's disjoint-line-pairs cap of 6 on corner-wedge clips holds regardless of the run split, since it only depends on which line-pairs get used, not on position — so a crude count of `6 (outside) + up to 3 (inside, reference data 20e)` doesn't immediately fall below 7 by itself; a naive per-run ceiling calculation can still reach 7 in some splits. The actual obstruction, if there is one, has to come from showing that achieving corner-wedge clips near the 6-cap forces the hull entry/exit points to sit at slope-order positions that make an interior N-clip in the remaining run impossible — a geometric compatibility question between the fixed cyclic order `1,2,...,13` and the two hull-crossing points, not a counting question. That's the real content turn 278's "ranking" needs to deliver and doesn't yet.

I'm not conceding anything here — nothing in turn 278 forces a concession, and this turn tightens the geometry against the weaving route rather than for it. My prior stands: the improved even-k bound is not tight at k=14, and the burden is now on showing a concrete hull entry/exit pair compatible with both a near-maximal corner-wedge harvest and at least one interior N-clip.

**Named next step, either of us:** locate, in the cyclic slope order `1,2,...,13`, where a line's hull-entry pair and hull-exit pair of crossings can sit relative to the 11 corner-wedge vertex-pairs, and whether any placement leaves both ≥4 corner-wedge clips available and a nonempty inside-run compatible with reference data 20's spacing.

## Turn 288 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-30T11:17:44Z

The general identity behind turn 287's arithmetic is worth stating cleanly, because it generalizes past `c=3` and it sharpens exactly the question PythagorAss just asked itself.

For any `k=14` arrangement with `p=0` and `c` triple points, `B = 168 - 3c`. Let `f` be the number of free (triangle-free) bounded segments, `s` the number serving exactly one triangle, `d` the number serving two (only possible where the far endpoint is a triple point, reference data 23c). Then `f+s+d=B` and `s+2d=3T` — counting segment-incidences two ways. Subtracting:

    d - f = 3T - B

At `T=54`: `3T=162`. So `d - f = 162 - (168-3c) = 3c - 6`.

- `c=0`: `d=0` always (no concurrence), so `f = 6`. But reference data 4's `p<=3` filter and reference data 22 together show `p=3` is required for `T<=54` to even be arithmetically live, and at `p=3` (Bader's family) `B=162`, giving `f=0` exactly — zero slack, which reference data 22 proves insertion into Kabanovitch's B cannot reach.
- `c=1`: `d-f=-3`, i.e. `f=d+3>=3`. Slack, no rigidity — but also no help, since three free segments is exactly Bader's own signature at 53, achieved with *no* concurrence at all. A single triple point buys nothing here that Bader doesn't already have.
- `c=2`: `d-f=0`. Every doubled segment must be matched by a free one elsewhere. No net gain in triangle-serving capacity from the concurrences themselves.
- `c=3`: `d-f=3`, minimized at `f=0, d=3`. This is turn 287's case, and it is the *only* one of the four where concurrence structurally lowers the saturation requirement below Bader's own `f=0` baseline — because it's the only one where `B` itself drops below `3T`.

## Turn 293 - PythagorAss - 2026-08-30T16:17:44Z

Turn 292's degree count assumes each triple point contributes exactly one doubled segment — the bridge line's 12th slot, copied straight from the degenerate k=4 example. That assumption is the actual load-bearing step, and it isn't the true local maximum. I ran the six-sector analysis agenda item 3 asked for, and it says the true cap is **two** doubled segments per isolated triple point, not one — which moves the c=3 budget from "stricter than Bader" to "exactly as loose as Bader."

**The six-sector picture.** At triple point P on lines a,b,c, the six rays from P sit in cyclic order c-,a+,b+,c+,a-,b- (each line contributes two opposite rays). A sector between two adjacent rays closes into a triangle `{x,y,L}` iff the nearest crossing along each bounding ray is the same line L. The middle ray of any three cyclically-consecutive rays is shared by two sectors, so its near-P segment doubles iff both flanking sectors close with the same L — i.e., iff L's forward-crossing arc from P (a fixed 180° half of directions, since L is a straight line not through P) contains all three of that triple's ray directions.

Reference data 23c's k=4 case realizes exactly one such triple (c-,a+,b+, using line 1 as L), doubling line a's single available segment. But k=4 only has one segment per line near P because there's nothing beyond it. At k=14, each of a,b,c has crossings on *both* sides of P, so the *opposite* triple (c+,a-,b-) is also available, and it is compatible: the two triples partition all six rays with no shared ray, so no line is asked for two different "nearest" identities on the same ray. A second helper line L''' whose forward arc covers `{c+,a-,b-}` (spanning 120°, fits in 180°) closes those two sectors too. Result: 4 of 6 sectors become triangles, 2 don't, and **both** of line a's P-adjacent segments — e(a+) and e(a-) — double. `d=2` at one isolated triple point, `f=0` locally, using two helper lines from the other eleven.

**Why it caps at 2, not 3.** Any *adjacent* triple (sharing a ray with the first, e.g. a+,b+,c+) would force nearest-on-c+ = L, but c+ and c- are antipodal and L's forward arc is exactly 180° — it can contain one of an antipodal pair, never both, generically. So only the two ray-disjoint opposite triples can fire simultaneously, and both always share the same middle line. Doubling is confined to one of the three lines, at two segments, never three lines or three segments.

**The corrected budget.** A triple point's bridge line gets `deg_T <= 13` (2 doubled + 9 ordinary, out of 11 total segments), not 12; its two flanking lines stay at `deg_T <= 11`, unchanged. For `c=3`: 3 bridge lines at 13, 6 flanking at 11, 5 untouched generic lines at 12. Sum `<= 39+66+60=165`, against `3T=162` needed — three slots of slack, matching `d=6, f=3` in turn 288's identity (`d-f=3c-6=3`). That is not a stricter ask than Bader's record, it's the *same* slack Bader already has (`f=3`), relocated from three ordinary segments to three doubled ones.

Turn 292's claim that `c=3` demands "more segments succeeding than Bader's own unbeaten construction" rests on the uncorrected `d<=1` cap and doesn't survive this. It isn't a construction yet — the two helper lines per point still have to fit consistently into one arrangement with eight other lines doing the rest of the work, and that global check is unstarted.

**Named next step, mine:** pick concrete coordinates for one triple point plus its two helper lines L, L''' realizing `d=2, f=0` locally, then check the two helper lines' other eleven crossings don't force a conflict at a second triple point's own helper-line assignment.

## Turn 307 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-31T05:18:44Z

The run-length rule turn 306 built is fine as bookkeeping, but the branch it flags as untested — "if that closure holds, `d_A` becomes 6" — is not untested. It's excluded, by the same mechanism that already caps the isolated case.

The general lemma underlying every ray computation on this table: sector `(r_a, r_b)` is triangular iff `nearest(r_a) = nearest(r_b)` — the two flanking rays' nearest crossings must be explained by one common line, which becomes the triangle's third side. A run of `L` consecutive triangular sectors forces `L+1` consecutive rays, cyclically, to share one nearest-identity. Point A's run of four (`S4,S5,S6,S1`) forces five consecutive rays — everything but position 3 — onto one value, `L_run`.

Six rays around a triple point split into three antipodal pairs, each three positions apart — a line's two rays are always opposite each other. Any five consecutive positions out of six necessarily contain two full antipodal pairs. Point A's run-of-four already forces agreement across line 1's pair (toward `B`, away from `B`) and line 3's pair (toward `C`, away). Both survive only because the "toward" ray in each pair ends at a chained triple point — `B={1,2,5}`, `C={3,5,6}` — which has two admissible line-identities, so the "away" ray's single ordinary nearest-line only has to match one of the two. That is reference data 27c's loophole, named but not pinned down until now.

Closing `S2` and `S3` to reach a full wrap needs one more ray added to the chain, and by pigeonhole that completes the third antipodal pair — line 4's. I read row 4 this turn: `2, [1,3], 6, 5` (`corpus/arrangements.json:214-222`), matching turn 304's citation. Both of line 4's far crossings from `A` are plain, un-bracketed entries — `V(4,2)` and `V(4,6)` are ordinary points, not triple points. Neither ray gets the dual-identity escape hatch. Closing the gap would require one single line to be nearest on both of line 4's opposite rays from `A` — exactly the configuration T293 proved impossible: an external line crosses line 4 at one point, lying on one ray or the other, never both. No spare line fixes this, because the obstruction isn't supply, it's that line 4's two neighbors are ordinary. Turn 306's named next step — attempt the single-line closure of `S2, S3` — is dead before it's tried.

This sharpens 27c rather than just blocking 306. A triple point in the two-of-three-lines-chained topology (the only one the corpus realizes) caps at `d=3` locally, not "`d=3` realized, ceiling unknown." A `c`-cycle of such points has `c` shared bridges, each double-counted in the local sums, so total `d = 3c - c = 2c` — matching the *isolated* formula exactly, not the `4.5c` crude bound 27c left open. Reference data 27a's `3T <= k(k-2) - c` therefore isn't scoped to isolated concurrences after all; it holds for cycle-chained ones too, on this topology, and `c=0` stays the strictly loosest regime for every chaining shape anyone has built or proposed.

## Turn 313 - Euclidn't - 2026-08-31T11:18:44Z

Turn 312's arithmetic is fine, but its framing of "fully saturated" as a set-membership fact — "twelve distinct triangles, no two sharing both other legs" — badly understates what saturation forces, and that gap is exactly where the p=0 program turn 312 is chasing gets expensive.

**The mutual-neighbor-lock lemma.** Let line `l` be fully saturated with row order `m_1, ..., m_n` (its `n` crossings in sequence, giving `n-1` bounded segments, all triangle sides). For any interior index `i` (`2 <= i <= n-1`), triangle `{l, m_{i-1}, m_i}` forces `l` and `m_{i-1}` adjacent in row `m_i` (the iff test, reference data 2), and triangle `{l, m_i, m_{i+1}}` forces `l` and `m_{i+1}` adjacent in row `m_i`. Since `l` occupies one position in row `m_i` with at most two neighbors, and both are now occupied, **`l`'s two neighbors in row `m_i` are exactly `m_{i-1}` and `m_{i+1}`, forced.** This holds for every interior partner of every saturated line — it needs nothing but the iff test and holds for any `k`, any table.

**Verified twice against Bader's own table, using only reference data 1's printed rows.** Line 1 is one of the eleven saturated lines (reference data 5: free segments sit on 8, 11, 12 only). Take `m_2 = 12` (interior). The lemma predicts `l=1`'s neighbors in row 12 are `m_1=14` and `m_3=13`. Row 12, printed in reference data 1: `11 8 2 9 4 10 5 6 3 7 14 1 13` — position 12 is `1`, flanked by `14` and `13`. **Matches exactly.** Take `m_3 = 13` (interior). Lemma predicts `1`'s neighbors in row 13 are `m_2=12` and `m_4=7`. Row 13: `11 2 8 4 9 5 10 3 6 14 7 1 12` — `1` sits between `7` and `12`. **Matches exactly.** (Python refused before execution again this session — `python3 -c "print('PYTHON OK')"` gated, twentieth consecutive day — so this is hand-verification from reference data 1's printed rows and reference data 2's printed list, not a tool run; both were already on the record before this turn.)

**Why this sharpens agenda item 4 against turn 312's route.** Turn 312 proposes checking whether a saturated line's "partner-set survives" a p=0 perturbation. The lemma shows survival of the partner *set* isn't the bar — for every one of a saturated line's ~11 interior partners, the *exact flanking pair* in that partner's own row is locked. The isolated cap of `d=2` is achieved by exactly two separate runs of length 2 (the antipodal pair `c+`/`c-`, each with its own flanking pair), giving `d = (2-1)+(2-1) = 2`. **Chained case:** a run of length 3 is legal the moment its middle ray's far endpoint is itself a triple point, since dual identity breaks the uniqueness step that produced the contradiction. `kobon_6_2`'s point `{1,3,4}` realizes `d=3`, consistent with either one run of 4 or two runs of 3+2 — either way it needs at least one run of length ≥3, confirming the block is broken exactly where a bridge ray sits.

Turn 326's `d_P<=6` ceiling is right, but "requires a hub surrounded by up to six neighboring triple points" is asserted, not derived — and it's wrong in both directions at once. Here is the actual minimum, and why even hitting it doesn't obviously work.

**The real lower bound is exactly three breaks, not six.** A "break" is a ray whose nearest-crossing point is itself a triple point, letting the two flanking sectors use different lines (27a's uniqueness argument fails there). Between two breaks, every ray is ordinary, and 27a's own chaining forces a *single* line to be nearest on the entire span from break to break — that's the same mechanism that gives the isolated `d<=2` cap. A span of `L+1` rays (L triangle sectors) is safe only if it avoids an antipodal pair; since any 4 consecutive rays out of 6 contain one (check all six rotations: `{0,1,2,3}` has `(0,3)`, `{1,2,3,4}` has `(1,4)`, etc.), a break-free span can cover at most 3 rays, i.e. 2 sectors. Six rays split among breaks with every gap `<=2` rays needs at least 3 breaks (with 2 breaks, the two gaps sum to 6 and pigeonhole forces one `>=3`, hitting the antipodal wall). So 3 is a **proven necessary condition**, and turn 326's "up to six" overstates the requirement with no derivation behind it — it's not even a claimed upper bound, just an unexamined guess.

**But three breaks is not obviously sufficient, and the natural attempt to build it fails outright.** The clean candidate: three hub lines through `P` (rays alternating break/ordinary as `a+, b-, c-` breaks) with three bridge lines `M1,M2,M3`, each break forced to be a point where `M_i, M_{i+1}` and the corresponding hub line concur. That configuration is always realizable, so line-count isn't the obstruction. But it doesn't give the full wrap: connecting `P` to the three vertices divides the triangle into exactly **three** sub-triangles (standard fact), which are the three *inward-facing* sectors. The three *outward* rays — the opposite direction of `a`, `b`, `c` — run away from the triangle into unbounded space, since nothing in this six-line picture closes them. Those three sectors are unbounded, not triangles. So the minimal, most natural realization of "three breaks" gives **`d_P = 0`**, not 6: the three triangle sectors that do exist are non-adjacent (each isolated between two unbounded sectors), and doubling needs adjacent pairs.

**So the honest state of agenda item 2 is this:** the proven floor is 3 breaks, the ceiling turn 326 named (6) was asserted not derived, and the one concrete attempt to hit even the floor produces zero doubling, not six. Closing the outward sectors needs additional structure beyond the minimal six-line gadget — more lines, which means more cost, which the arithmetic hasn't absorbed. ## Turn 346 - Euclidn't - 2026-09-01T19:19:44Z

Turn 345's C7 argument is correct but incomplete even on its own turf, and the mechanism generalizes far past k=14. I generalize it properly and apply it fresh to k=18 and k=20, which nobody has touched with this tool.

**The lemma.** Let a k-line arrangement be invariant under rotation by `2π/n` about a point `O` that is not a vertex of the arrangement, `n > 2`. For a triangle `T` fixed setwise by the generator `g`, `g` induces a permutation of `T`'s three vertices, giving a homomorphism from the cyclic stabilizer `H = Stab(T) ≤ Z_n` into `S_3`. Since `H` is cyclic, its image is cyclic, hence of order 1, 2, or 3.

- Order 1 (fixes all three vertices pointwise): forces the group element to fix 3 distinct points, so it's the identity — only `H` trivial survives.
- Order 2 (a transposition, fixing one vertex pointwise, swapping the other two): the fixed vertex must equal `O`, since a nontrivial rotation fixes only its center. Excluded by genericity.
- Order 3 (a 3-cycle, fixing none pointwise): needs no vertex at `O`. Requires `3 | n`.

So generically, `Stab(T)` is trivial or (only if `3|n`) the unique subgroup of order 3. Orbit sizes are `n`, or `n/3` when `3|n` — nothing else. **`T ≡ 0 (mod n)` if `3∤n`, and `T ≡ 0 (mod n/3)` if `3|n`.** Turn 345's `n=7` case is the `3∤n` branch and needed no genericity caveat at all — 7 is odd, so the order-2 exclusion never arises. It's already complete as stated; I'm not correcting it, only noting why it dodged the caveat that matters elsewhere.

**k=14, extended.** `n=7`: `T≡0 mod7`, `54 mod7=5`: dead (T345's case). `n=14`, which T345 didn't check: `3∤14`, `T≡0 mod14`, `54 mod14=12`: also dead. Both nontrivial divisors of 14 above 2 are excluded.

On my own assignment: item 3, `C3` at `k=18`. Reference data 32e pins `s ∈ {1,4}`, one or four concentric equilateral faces. Here is why `s=4` is impossible, and it needs no coordinates, only the standard incircle-containment fact.

**Lemma.** No two distinct `C3`-fixed candidate triangles can both be faces of the arrangement.

A `C3`-fixed triangle is invariant under 120° rotation about `O`, hence equilateral with `O` as centroid = incenter. Since the rotation is an isometry fixing `O`, it maps each bounding line to the next, so all three lines sit at one common distance `ρ` from `O` — the triangle's inradius — and the incircle of radius `ρ` about `O` is contained in the closed triangle, touching only the three sides.

Take two candidates `T_k` (orbit `k`, inradius `ρ_k`) and `T_j` (orbit `j`, inradius `ρ_j`), both claimed as faces, `k≠j`.

- If `ρ_k < ρ_j`: each line of orbit `k` sits at distance `ρ_k` from `O`, strictly less than `ρ_j`, so it crosses the open disk of radius `ρ_j` about `O` — a line at distance `d` from a circle's center meets the open disk iff `d <` radius. That disk lies inside `T_j`. So an orbit-`k` line passes through `T_j`'s interior, and `T_j` is not an uncut face. Contradiction.
- If `ρ_k = ρ_j = ρ`: both triangles share one incircle but are rotated relative to each other by some `φ ∈ (0°,120°)` (distinct orbits, distinct lines). A side of `T_k`, tangent to the shared incircle at angle `φ`, touches that circle at a point that is *not* one of `T_j`'s three tangency points (those sit at `0°,120°,240°` relative to `T_j`), hence lies in `T_j`'s open interior (the incircle touches `T_j`'s boundary only at the three tangency points; every other circle point is strictly inside). The tangent line passes through that interior point. Contradiction.

Either way, two distinct orbits cannot both survive as faces. So **`s ≤ 1`** unconditionally. Combined with `s ≡ 94 ≡ 1 (mod 3)` and `0 ≤ s ≤ 6`, the only value satisfying both `s≤1` and `s≡1 mod 3` is `s = 1`. **`s = 4` is dead; `C3` at `k=18` requires exactly one fixed equilateral face, not one-or-four.**

This sharpens reference data 32e but does not close item 3: the surviving requirement is that the other five orbits' candidate triangles must each be cut by some other line, which is generically easy and proves nothing yet either way. I attempted the verifier for a numeric sanity check of the tangent-line computation; blocked at approval, so `verifier_runs` is empty and the argument above stands on the incircle-containment fact alone, which is elementary and checkable by hand.

## Turn 361 - Euclidn't - 2026-09-02T09:17:44Z

Turn 360's scope correction is fair and doesn't need a concession from me: T359 proved the *convex* and *interior-point* order types of four points both force a self-cut among the six pairwise connectors, killing K4 outright at c=4. It says nothing about which proper subset of fifteen pairs survives on six points, and PythagorAss is right that the prism and K_{3,3} only need nine of fifteen. But one of those two candidates dies immediately, by a mechanism I hadn't used yet and that needs no coordinates at all.

A bridge edge between two triple points P, Q is, by definition (reference data 27a/29), the bounded segment of the line through P and Q with no other arrangement line crossing it in between. If two bridge edges — say P1P2 and P3P4, four distinct triple points — cross each other as bounded straight segments at a point interior to both, that point lies on line(P1,P2) strictly between P1 and P2, and it lies there *because* line(P3,P4) passes through it. Line(P3,P4) is a line of the arrangement. So the crossing disqualifies segment P1P2 as an uncut bridge, and symmetrically disqualifies P3P4. This is independent of the cevian-extension mechanism T358 and T359 used (a bridge line's *extension beyond its own endpoints* cutting a different bridge) — it's a plain segment-segment crossing between two edges of the bridge graph itself, drawn as a straight-line diagram on the c triple points.

So: for every edge of a proposed bridge graph to survive as an uncut bridge simultaneously, the graph must admit a drawing on those points, using literal straight segments between the specified pairs, with **zero crossings among its own edges**.
